strengths: Addresses a highly critical and under-examined area: safety alignment and defense in video large language models (Video LLMs).

Introduces VideoSafetyBench (VSB-77k), a comprehensive, culturally diverse benchmark comprising over 77,000 video-query pairs across 19 subcategories, which is a valuable resource for future research.

Proposes an innovative dual-stage post-training framework, VideoSafety-R1, combining explicit alarm tokens (AT-SFT) and Safety-Guided GRPO with Dynamic Reward Adaptation to enable active safety reasoning.

Provides extensive experimental evaluations, demonstrating massive improvements in Defense Success Rate (+65.1%) and strong generalization to image safety benchmarks, while keeping degradation in standard video understanding benchmarks to a minimum.
Explores interesting dimensions such as the effect of frame rate (FPS) on model safety and visual-textual cross-modality safety vulnerabilities.
weaknesses: The defense framework significantly increases the False Refusal Rate (FRR) on benign queries, jumping from 0.7% on the baseline to 13.4% on VideoSafety-R1. This over-defensiveness/over-refusal behavior is a noticeable trade-off that limits real-world deployability.

The methodology description in Section 4.2 regarding how the rule-based safety reward is calculated for GRPO could be presented with more mathematical precision, specifically the exact reward values assigned for Correct_v and Correct_t.

While the cost-effectiveness and accuracy of the Qwen-Long evaluator are validated against human experts on a subset (Table 7), utilizing an automatic LLM judge as the sole evaluator across the full benchmark can still introduce bias. A broader human evaluation of the final model's safety and helpfulness would strengthen the claims.

strengths: The paper addresses a critical and under-explored security gap: the safety degradation in Large Language Models when transitioning from text-only to multimodal video inputs.

The proposed VideoSafetyBench (VSB-77k) is the first large-scale, multilingual, and culturally diverse benchmark specifically tailored for assessing Video LLM safety, spanning 19 subcategories across 10 language communities.

The proposed VideoSafety-R1 defense framework introduces highly effective innovations: Alarm Token-Guided Safety Fine-Tuning (AT-SFT) for proactive harm perception and Safety-Guided GRPO with rule-based rewards for active reasoning.

The empirical results are outstanding, showing a massive defense success rate improvement on VSB-Eval-HH (+65.1%) and substantial generalization gains on image safety benchmarks (+59.1% on MMBench), while preserving core video-understanding capabilities (less than 1% degradation on general video benchmarks).
Extremely thorough and detailed appendix, including human evaluation verification of the LLM-as-a-judge metric, ablation studies on helpfulness, and clear qualitative comparisons.
weaknesses: Integrating the learned visual and textual alarm tokens requires minor architectural and sequence formatting modifications, which may complicate direct plug-and-play usage of VideoSafety-R1 in off-the-shelf serving frameworks compared to post-hoc wrapping or purely prompt-based defenses.

The evaluation strongly relies on a commercial API (Qwen-Long) as the safety judge. Even though the authors provide an elegant cost-effectiveness and reliability study comparing various models in the appendix, the closed-source nature of the evaluator might pose reproducibility challenges over time as APIs evolve.
As acknowledged in the limitations, the final generated safety reasoning and safe responses can occasionally sound repetitive and robotic compared to natural human writing.

The paper lacks a discussion on the computational resources (e.g., GPU hours, training wall-clock time) required for the multi-stage post-training pipeline (SFT followed by GRPO), which is important for understanding the practical overhead of the defense.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly critical and under-explored safety gap in Video Large Language Models (Video LLMs), demonstrating that integrating video modality severely degrades safety alignment (exposing a significant 'modality safety tax').

The introduction of VideoSafetyBench (VSB-77k), containing over 77k video-query pairs across 19 safety subcategories and 10 distinct language communities, represents a valuable, large-scale, and culturally diverse dataset contribution.

The proposed VideoSafety-R1 post-training defense is novel and well-designed, effectively combining supervised learning via multimodal alarm tokens (AT-SFT) with reinforcement learning (Safety-Guided GRPO) and a Dynamic Reward Adaptation mechanism.

The empirical evaluation is exceptionally thorough, demonstrating massive safety improvements on multiple benchmarks (VSB-Eval, MMBench, VLGuard, FigStep) while showing minimal degradation on general video understanding capabilities (MVBench, VideoMME).
weaknesses: The qualitative safety reasoning and responses generated by VideoSafety-R1 (shown in Figures 9-12) are highly robotic, repetitive, and sometimes logically circular. For example, in Figure 12, the model outputs awkward phrasing like 'its classification as unrelated does not affect the fact that the question is unrelated' and 'This situation requires a response from me, which cannot occur due to the inherent inability to respond'. This indicates that the CoT templates used for dataset generation and policy optimization enforce overly rigid and unnatural response patterns.

The data curation, prompt generation, and evaluation pipelines heavily rely on proprietary commercial APIs (such as Qwen-Max, Qwen-Max-VL, Qwen-Long, and GPT-4o). This creates a reproducibility bottleneck, as commercial model APIs can undergo silent updates, drift over time, or be restricted due to regional availability.

The technical integration of visual alarm tokens (Eq. 1) lacks architectural clarity. Because different Video LLMs employ varied vision-language projection layers, it is unclear whether the visual alarm tokens are appended to visual features before or after the projection layer, and how easily this component adapts to heterogeneous connector designs.

In Equation 6, the reference policy ($\pi_{\text{ref}}$) used in the KL divergence constraint is not explicitly defined. Clarification on whether $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ refers to the base model, the post-SFT (AT-SFT) model, or another checkpoint would greatly enhance reproducibility.

strengths: Compelling and highly timely topic: Systematic safety evaluation and defense in Video Large Language Models (Video LLMs), which is currently under-studied compared to Image LLMs.

Comprehensive benchmark: VideoSafetyEval (VSE) is a large-scale, real-world benchmark featuring 11.4k video-query pairs across 19 risk categories and 10 language communities, providing a solid foundation for future research.

Innovative defense framework: VideoSafety-R1 effectively combines Alarm Token-Guided SFT (AT-SFT) and Safety-guided GRPO. The use of safety-aware thinking chains (inspired by DeepSeek-R1) and dynamic reward adaptation (DRA) is technically sound and highly effective.

Extensive evaluation and analysis: The paper includes a zero-shot evaluation of 21 Video LLMs, demonstrating a critical drop in safety when video modality is introduced. It also provides excellent analytical insights, such as the attention sink shift and the decoupling of token load vs. semantic richness.
Highly detailed appendix: Includes extensive dataset statistics, prompts, human verification, case studies, and exact training details, ensuring reproducibility.
weaknesses: Complexity of the pipeline: The training process of VideoSafety-R1 is complex, spanning four distinct stages (alarm token initialization, SFT, CoT cold-start, and GRPO reinforcement). This might make it difficult to implement and tune for smaller research labs.

Heavy reliance on proprietary commercial models: Both the dataset annotation (using Qwen-Max-VL) and the evaluation (using Qwen-Long API) rely heavily on closed-source APIs. Although the authors validate these with human evaluation, open-source alternatives for annotation and evaluation would be preferred.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly critical and under-explored area: safety evaluation and defense in Video Large Language Models (Video LLMs).
The creation of VideoSafetyEval (VSE), a large-scale safety benchmark containing 11.4k video-query pairs across 19 subcategories and 10 languages, provides a valuable resource for the community.
The paper presents an extensive empirical study evaluating 21 mainstream Video LLMs, demonstrating a systematic safety degradation (averaging 34.2%) when the video modality is introduced.

The proposed VideoSafety-R1 framework successfully introduces reasoning-based defense (using Chain-of-Thought and GRPO) to visual safety, shifting safety alignment from simple perception to active verification.
weaknesses: Heavy Reliance on Synthetic/LLM-Generated Data: The dataset construction pipeline relies heavily on LLMs (GPT-4o, Qwen-Max-VL, Qwen-Long) for video filtering, clip annotation, and query generation. Despite some human verification, this heavily synthetic pipeline risks propagating LLM-intrinsic biases and unrealistic user behaviors into the benchmark.

Significant Over-Defense / High False Refusal Rate (FRR): Table 2 shows that after applying VideoSafety-R1, the False Refusal Rate of VideoLLaMA3-2B on safe queries (VSE-SafeQ) increases from 0.7% to 13.4%. This 12.7% absolute increase in false refusals indicates that the model becomes overly conservative, significantly damaging its utility.

Substantial Inference Latency: As discussed in Section I, the CoT ('think') mode doubles the inference latency (11.80s vs. 5.12s) compared to the direct response mode due to the generation of extra reasoning tokens. This latency overhead is a major bottleneck for real-time video moderation or deployment in production systems.

Incremental Technical Novelty: The core technical components of VideoSafety-R1 are largely integrations of existing methods. GRPO is adapted from recent reasoning paradigms (DeepSeek), and the use of special/alarm tokens for safety classification is closely related to existing prefix-tuning and guardrail token techniques.

Potential Evaluation Bias from LLM Judges: The primary metric for safety (DSR) and helpfulness (SHelp) relies on Qwen-Long as a judge. LLM-as-a-judge evaluations are susceptible to verbosity bias, formatting preferences, and may not fully capture subtle evasions or jailbreaks compared to comprehensive human evaluation.

strengths: Highly timely and important topic: Video LLM safety is a critically under-explored area compared to static image safety.
Large-scale, well-designed benchmark (VideoSafetyEval): 11.4k pairs across 19 subcategories, covering 10 language communities, based on real-world guidelines (YouTube/TikTok).
Solid defense framework (VideoSafety-R1): Synergizes Alarm Token-Guided SFT (AT-SFT) with Safety-guided GRPO, shifting video safety defense from passive perception to active reasoning.

Comprehensive evaluation: Tests 21 mainstream Video LLM variants and reports substantial improvements (+71.1% on VSE-HH) with very minimal degradation on standard video understanding benchmarks (0.66% average drop).

In-depth analytical insights: Disentangles the effect of frame counts vs. semantic harmfulness and provides a fascinating attention sink analysis showing how the proposed alarm tokens shift visual attention back to textual safety anchors.
weaknesses: Reliance on Qwen-Long API as the evaluator: The safety evaluation heavily depends on Qwen-Long. Although validated against human annotators in Appendix J, API updates and potential evaluation biases could affect reproducibility.

Rigidity of the VideoSafetyThinking (VST) dataset: Since the thinking chains are generated using template-driven prompting on Qwen-Max, the safety reasoning might be repetitive or lack the nuance and flexibility of genuine human reasoning.
Single alarm token limitation: Appending a single global alarm token at the end of sequences may struggle with long-form video inputs where harmful cues are highly localized or sparse across frames.

High computational complexity of RL training: Training reinforcement learning (GRPO) on video-text pairs is notoriously expensive. While the authors provide some FLOPs estimates, practical deployment details like training VRAM and wall-clock times are less explored.
